newsitem.title: INDIA: Gandhians meet high-tech at India anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Gandhians meet high-tech at India anniversary.

text.p: The master of ceremonies sounded crisp: "For everything you say about India, the opposite is also true."

A late night show in New Delhi on Thursday to mark the 50th anniversary of India's independence from British rule displayed a nation which has one eye on high technology and another on an ancient culture.
Pop stars crooned westernised versions of patriotic songs, watched by thousands of youngsters in jeans and T-shirts at Vijay Chowk (Victory Square).
They were just a hundred metres (yards) away from parliament, where leaders gathered to pay tributes to austere nationalist leader Mahatma Gandhi.
"It is all so beautiful," gushed Reshma, a young woman wearing glasses.
The show was organised by Wizcraft, which last year managed a concert by pop star Michael Jackson.

Squatting on the grass, wearing freshly-dusted military uniforms and medals were a few veterans from the Indian National Army (INA), a rebellious group that fought British rule by siding with Germany during World War Two.
"The country should not lose its way. We can still make it a heaven," said Shobha Singh, who said he had been a personal bodyguard for INA leader Subhas Chandra Bose.
On the stage, A.R. Rahaman, often called a musical whizkid, crooned in his trademark fusion of western and Indian tunes.

Sitting on sofas laid out across the Raj Path boulevard were Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and five of his predecessors in office, H.D. Deve Gowda, Atal Behari Vajpayee, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Chandra Shekhar and V.P. Singh.
Later, laser projectors beamed simulated fireworks in the colours of India's national flag, saffron, white and green.
Gujral received national flags on stage from a contigent of independence campaigners. One of them was dressed like Mahatma Gandhi.
"They belong to the generation whch made sacrifices," Gujral said. "Let us promise we will not let them down."
"We have been successful, we will be successful," he said.

Thousands of people, many of them ageing veterans of the independence movement, earlier joined a "March of the Nation" that culminated at the square located before the presidential palace on the Raisina Hill.
A truck depicting green-fatigued soldiers guarding the Himalayan mountains whizzed past a stage where colourfully dressed dancers performed folk dances.
Tableaux showcased India's provincial cultures. Families gathered around vast green lawns, flanked on both sides by key government buildings illuminated with stunning rows of lights.
